entries.title: Maryland Supreme Court Allows Redistricting Ballot Question to Move Forward
entries.summary: The court said the amendment needs to be redrafted before being presented to voters in November.
entries.content:
The Maryland Supreme Court on Thursday allowed Democrats’ much-debated redistricting amendment to appear on ballots in November.

Voters will decide whether to change the state constitution to allow lawmakers to draw legislative and congressional districts without facing stringent compactness standards in the future — marking a win for state Democrats who passed the amendment last month.

Thursday’s ruling reversed an earlier county circuit-court decision that concluded the ballot measure was flawed because it poses multiple redistricting questions to voters.

The proposition will need to be redrafted before being presented to voters, the state Supreme Court said, including adding a clarification that the state constitution does not provide “applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.”

Lawmakers must also say the constitution’s standards only apply to Maryland General Assembly districts, not congressional ones.

A “yes” vote would give the state Supreme Court the sole authority to hear these cases first before the traditional lower-court appeals process.

Maryland joined a wave of Democratic states that launched redistricting efforts in reaction to President Donald Trump’s push for Republicans to flip additional House seats ahead of this year’s midterms. The state’s new map, which would favor Democrats in all eight House districts, would not go into effect until at least 2028.

Nicole Beus Harris, the chair of the Maryland Republican Party, said she was disappointed by the court’s decision to allow “a reworded gerrymandering amendment" on the ballot, she wrote on X. 

“Nevertheless, we are confident we can defeat this amendment at the ballot box in November,” she said.

entries.title: Daylen Lile, Nationals Cornerstone?
entries.summary: The 23-year old outfielder is in the middle of a (very) hot streak.
entries.content:
Daylen Lile has been crushing the ball, which led me to ask him about signs — as in, any sign that he’s completely dialed in — at his locker last week. He did not, to my surprise, talk about something like his timing with fastballs, nor did he mention a recent home run that landed in the second deck at Nationals Park. Instead he pointed to a single pitch.

On Aug. 24, Ryan Feltner, a righty for the Rockies, threw Lile an 85-mph changeup on the low-and-outside corner. Lile, a 23-year-old outfielder, thought for a millisecond about swinging but didn’t. The umpire called strike one. And because Lile resisted, he knew he was in one of his zones, when the game slows down enough for him to rake (and rake, and rake). It was, in other words, a sign.

Two pitches later, Feltner threw a more manageable changeup and Lile roped it for a double. In his next at-bat, he singled. In the at-bat after that, he crushed that second-deck homer.

"Whenever I'm taking the pitcher's best pitch, when I’m laying off it pretty easy, tracking it all the way, that’s when I know I’m dialed in,” Lile told me. “A good take is really all it is.”

If that sounds simple, it isn’t — especially for a player who unmercifully assesses himself with a microscope. Lile is an unforgiving self-described perfectionist, which is extra hard when facing the “one percent of the one percent,” as he put it. But the theme of his season, his first full one in the majors, is figuring out how to better process struggles big and small. As a rookie last year, he mostly excelled, a smooth continuation of the rest of his baseball life. Wherever he’d played, whenever he’d played, he had hit. That’s generally how you wind up in the big leagues before you can rent a car without underage fees.

This year, though, has been different. Yes, right now, Lile’s in the middle of a loud, elongated up of an up-and-down season. He was just named National League player of the week, posting three homers, two doubles, five walks and a 1.533 on-base-plus-slugging percentage between Aug. 24 and 30. He homered twice against the Marlins on Monday. He’s once again proving, as the Nats plot future rosters, that he could be a major contributor. It’s felt like a second arrival.

But his chase rate is still in the ninth percentile among all hitters, according to Statcast, which is evidence that Lile’s been swinging at bad pitches throughout the year, mostly when he’s been frustrated and putting too much pressure on every at-bat. In 2025, by contrast, in a smaller sample of games, he was in the 56th percentile and that showed in his results. His production typically follows his plate discipline, which is to say that he’s productive when he can quiet his busy mind.

It’s the most relatable thing about a person who can hit a baseball 420 feet. Also relatable: Even when he thrives at the highest level of his field, Lile finds reasons to shake his head, to nitpick, to wish he had done just a little bit more (or, in some cases, less). Early success both accelerated his career and complicated the stories he tells himself. He’s learning, tough, trying like mad to think less. For a team out of another playoff race, it’s the next-best way to use this time of year.

“I would say I kind of got spoiled with August and September last season,” Lile said. “But, you know, I really haven’t had many ups and downs in my career, and this year I’ve had this roller coaster of the middle, then up, middle, down, up, middle, down, down, up. So I’m trying to just compete as much as possible and not really think out there.”

I first started covering the Nationals in late 2018, which means I’ve been thinking about them, in one way or another, for most of the last decade (with a break and job change mixed in). When you’re around a team that long, there are a handful of random snippets that really stick to your brain — sometimes for explainable reasons, sometimes not. For me, this includes a passing conversation in August or September of 2022, after the Nationals traded Juan Soto.

Naturally, I’d asked a member of the front office about the future, about who might anchor the next winning team in D.C., whenever that came. James Wood basically jumped out of his mouth, the obvious answer. Cade Cavalli, too, who he believed would grow into an ace. But the third name surprised me, if only because it wasn’t CJ Abrams, whom they’d just acquired in the Soto deal, or Dylan Crews, whom the Nats had taken with the second pick in the draft that summer.

“Lile?” I remember asking. He hadn’t stuttered. At that point, Lile was in his first full summer in the Nationals’ minor league system. They drafted him out of high school with their second pick in 2021, a round after Brady House. From the beginning, Lile was described to me as a pure hitter, a teenager with the critical gift of making lots of contact. He also was — and still is — very fast. A Wood- or Cavalli-level cornerstone, though, was a few steps above the steady praise I had heard.

This made me follow Lile’s career through a narrow lens: That good? Part of the amorphous core that will eventually bring the Nationals back from the dead? To be clear, these aren’t fair measures for any player. But in the years since, Lile has kept justifying his inclusion in that discussion, starting with his breakout debut in 2025. In 91 games, he hit 11 triples and had an .845 OPS. He was named National League Player of the Month for September. He then finished fifth in Rookie of the Year voting.

And then this year has tested his brain as much as his bat or glove. June felt like a low. Moving forward, Lile wants to walk a lot more, which comes back to not chasing so many pitches out of the zone. Chris Burke, his offseason hitting coach in Louisville, played six seasons in the major leagues. After the way Lile finished last season, Burke knew he had set a crazy bar for himself, especially now that pitchers would be circling Lile’s name on scouting reports.

“I actually tried to caution him a little bit,” Burke told me. “Like, don’t let that be your standard, that’s not really fair. But part of what makes him special is that he is not easily impressed by himself. I think he believes he can be one of the best hitters in the world. And, you know, he's clearly proven that's in there.”

Over the winter, the two of them talked all this through, sometimes spending about half of their hour-long sessions on the mental side of the game. And with Lile heading home again soon, the recent leap in his numbers, helped by his August tear, could reset the bar at an unreasonable height. But expectations, however light or heavy, are the burden every professional athlete wants. For Lile, they also come as the Nats are trying to turn the corner to competitive, meaning the team is hoping to arrive and stick in a similar way.

Wood, back this week from an oblique injury, remains the most important piece of the Next Core. Abrams has a less certain future with the team, though he’s shown he can hit like a full-on star (no matter where he plays in the field). Cavalli, as predicted, is turning into an ace, if he’s not there already. There are blue-chip prospects in the minors, including Eli Willits, the No. 1 pick in 2024, and Chris Hacopian, the team’s first-round choice this summer. But it would still mean a lot for the Nationals if Lile was a logical addition to this list.

“I want to finish stronger than how I did in the first half and actually leave people like, ‘OK, he is the player we thought he was,’” Lile said. When I asked who he meant by “people,” he paused and furrowed his brows, a regular expression for him. At points this season, the voice inside his head had wondered if he was good enough, if he belonged in the majors, if the end of last year was just a burst of good luck, a mirage.

“Well, myself,” he said. “That’s the biggest one.”

entries.title: Survivors of Epstein’s Abuse Say They Feel Snubbed by the DOJ
entries.summary: Weeks after a meeting with Todd Blanche, survivors and advocates say they’re losing hope that the attorney general will probe the late sex offender’s network.
entries.content:
Outspoken survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse say Justice Department officials have not taken meaningful steps to follow up on their meeting with Todd Blanche in the weeks since he became attorney general.

Blanche sat down with them at DOJ headquarters in July, when his Senate confirmation hung in the balance, in what was described as an “initial” effort to hear their concerns. The survivors say the lack of communication from officials since then has only reinforced their belief that a Blanche-led department has no intention of pursuing the issues they brought to him.

“There’s just not an interest,” Annie Farmer, one of the survivors, said in an interview. “They want to move on and turn the page.”

Even a general commitment to following new leads, interviewing new witnesses or investigating potential suspects in Epstein’s vast network of rich and powerful men would be seen as a positive sign, survivors said.

So would a promise to address what survivors said were errors in the release of files from the Epstein case, including a failure to redact their personal information and withholding the names of possible co-conspirators and other important details.

“Literally, you could take any avenue and just say, ‘Good, we will move on this one thing and start there,’” said Dani Bensky, a survivor who testified at Blanche’s confirmation hearing. “I think any of us would have been like, ‘OK, at least they’re doing something, and at least we were heard,’ instead of this defensive, gaslighting experience.’”

The Justice Department declined to answer questions about its interactions with survivors, the status of investigations related to Epstein and staffing of Epstein-related inquiries. An unsigned emailed statement from the department said, “We have responded to all requests for meetings w/ victims and/or their advocates.”

Epstein died in federal custody in 2019 while facing federal sex-trafficking charges in what authorities ruled a suicide. His longtime accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, was convicted of helping him groom, abuse and traffic underage girls and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.

The survivors had spent months pushing for a meeting. They hoped Blanche, who in the department’s No. 2 role had overseen the release of Epstein records under a law passed by Congress, would offer some reassurance that the DOJ would take seriously their demands for greater accountability and transparency around the late sex offender’s case.

The meeting came together hastily on the second day of his confirmation hearing to lead the Justice Department. Blanche had initially resisted pressure from lawmakers to sit down with survivors. But Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) threatened to hold up Blanche’s nomination in the Judiciary Committee unless he spoke face-to-face with a group of survivors who had traveled to Washington to attend the proceeding.

Bensky had testified that morning, recounting to lawmakers how the department had failed to redact her personal information from three batches of files and criticizing Blanche for ignoring repeated requests for an in-person discussion.

Soon after the hearing adjourned, Bensky said, a Justice Department staffer pulled her aside and proposed a meeting with Alessandra Serano, a longtime sex crimes prosecutor whom Blanche had recently appointed to lead the DOJ’s anti-human-trafficking efforts.

Bensky said she told the staffer: “We're not meeting with anybody but Blanche.”

After a scramble to coordinate schedules, Bensky and others were summoned to a 4:30 p.m. meeting at department headquarters. About half a dozen survivors attended. Joining virtually were their lawyers and advocates from the anti-trafficking organization World Without Exploitation, which represents many Epstein survivors. Blanche, Serano, FBI agents and other DOJ officials were present.

In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson called the meeting a “productive, initial discussion.” Blanche had walked the participants through what was needed for investigations to proceed and encouraged victims to meet with FBI investigators as a next step, according to the statement.

Survivors, however, came away feeling deflated and dismissed.

With little time to prepare for the meeting, Bensky said the group had decided to focus on a few key issues, including the Justice Department’s decision not to follow up on certain investigative leads and the process for redacting survivors’ information from the Epstein files.

They also asked Blanche to explain why the Justice Department had transferred Maxwell to a minimum-security prison camp during the height of uproar over the release of the files last year, according to Bensky.

Blanche bristled at many of their questions, survivors said, leaving them with the impression that he was interested in little more than shoring up support for his nomination.

Tillis, satisfied that the meeting had taken place, later voted to confirm Blanche. A spokesperson for the senator didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In the weeks since, survivors and their representatives say they’ve come to view Blanche’s suggestion that they go to the FBI as particularly problematic. Many survivors have already spoken with FBI investigators, some of them years ago when the most critical details of their abuse were fresh in their minds, they said.

Some worry they could undermine investigations if they were to sit for new FBI interviews and their recollections don’t line up perfectly with their original reports.

“To ask them to go back to the FBI is very disingenuous,” said Rebecca Zipkin, the policy director at World Without Exploitation and a former sex crimes prosecutor in Brooklyn. “Appropriate procedure would be for them to be reviewing all of the original FBI reports, seeing who was never followed up with, who should be followed up with, and assigning prosecutors and FBI agents who already were involved with this case.”

At the same time, Blanche’s elevation of Serano, whose mandate involves coordinating efforts to stop child exploitation and human trafficking, has brought the group some cautious optimism. Serano spent nearly two decades focusing on trafficking and sex-crime cases as a federal prosecutor, winning national recognition for her prosecutions. Zipkin said she held her work in high regard.

But Serano’s specific responsibilities with respect to the Epstein case aren’t clear, according to Zipkin.

Zipkin described a conversation with Serano on Zoom on July 20 as respectful and constructive overall, but she said Serano was limited in what she shared about the Justice Department’s plans.

“We were hoping that her position would be to work on opening investigations,” Zipkin said. “I didn't get confirmation on that either way.”

The Justice Department did not respond to questions seeking to clarify Serano’s duties or make her available for an interview.

Zipkin and survivors noted that, despite an exodus of highly experienced DOJ attorneys and investigators, many staffers with deep knowledge of the Epstein case remain. They questioned why Justice Department leaders appeared not to have tapped those officials for roles similar to Serano’s.

Ideally, Zipkin said, they want to see a coordinated effort among federal prosecutors’ offices in New York, New Mexico, Florida and the Virgin Islands — places where Epstein is known to have committed crimes — to open investigations into people named in the files who had been closely involved with Epstein.

They’re also seeking accountability — or at least an explanation from justice officials — for the department’s years of failure to act on reports of Epstein’s abuse, including a 1996 complaint by Farmer’s sister that went uninvestigated for decades.

Farmer, whose sister was among the first people to report Epstein’s crimes to the FBI, said there’s precedent for such a move. In 2021, justice officials probed the mishandling of FBI reports related to serial sex abuse by Larry Nassar, the doctor for the U.S. women’s gymnastics team.

“I think that some people don't appreciate the fact that, for my sister, their refusal to even acknowledge that her report had been made for so many years and silence on the issue was very damaging,” Farmer said. “Why wouldn’t you do what you’ve done in the past?”

Absent DOJ action, survivors say they are putting their faith in Congress and state authorities to probe many of the leads they say the federal government should have already taken up.

They lauded the House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer for listening to survivors, interviewing key witnesses in Epstein’s network and referring two Epstein associates to the Justice Department for investigation. Comer signaled last month that the committee may soon make criminal referrals in the case.

Benksy and Farmer said they were also encouraged by the New Mexico Department of Justice’s recently renewed investigation into alleged crimes at Epstein’s Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County.

State authorities sued Blanche and the Department of Justice last month, seeking unredacted Epstein case files they say may help identify victims, witnesses and previously unexamined crimes at the 8,000-acre property. The Justice Department said last month that it was not required to turn over the documents.

entries.title: ‘This Place Doesn’t Have to Work This Way’
entries.summary: Bipartisan lawmakers appeal to party leaders to change basic House functions.
entries.content:
Rank-and-file lawmakers have a surprising amount of bipartisan overlap when it comes to ideas about how to make Congress work even just a little bit better.

Take Reps. Chrissy Houlahan and Randy Fine, a Pennsylvania Democrat and Florida Republican who rarely agree on anything. On Wednesday, they were among the dozen lawmakers offering input at the House Rules Committee “member day” hearing. It’s a biennial event that resembles an open-mic night — anyone can offer up ideas they think will make the House function more efficiently.

Houlahan, an Air Force veteran serving on the House Intelligence Committee, proposed mandatory training for all lawmakers on how to handle classified information. She considers the current lack of training a glaring oversight given how many lawmakers come to Washington with no background in national security.

Next up, Fine interrupted his introduction to second Houlahan’s idea. A former casino, tech and health industry executive, Fine sheepishly admitted that he assumed security officials forgot to give him his training on sensitive material because of the unusual circumstances of his arrival.

“I thought I didn’t get any training on classified information because I came in in a special election,” said Fine, who was sworn in in April 2025.

This proposal gained a third vote of confidence later from Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans, a former Navy helicopter pilot who represents thousands of military workers in Virginia’s shipyard-heavy Hampton Roads region.

Many constituents undergo more training and have mandatory updates for handling intelligence, Kiggans said. “We have none of that here in Congress!”

It was one of more than a couple dozen proposals that came from the lawmakers testifying before the panel tasked with crafting a package of rules at the start of each new Congress.

Member day doesn’t get much attention because it’s so much inside baseball about the machinations of Congress, but the ideas put forth demonstrate how much lawmakers recognize the broken nature of their end of the Capitol.

Even with these modest proposals, the lawmakers were sending a message that they want to shift more power away from the leadership suites in the Capitol and across the street to the House office buildings, where the rank-and-file toil away on their committee work.

Houlahan came into office with the majority-making class of 2018 Democrats, who really believed they could change Congress. Almost eight years later, she’s run up against resistance from both Democratic and Republican majorities. Seemingly easy fixes like changing the voting and committee hearing calendars for more debate and member participation have languished.

And that’s left the average lawmaker feeling as if they’re chasing their own tails every day.

“The reason why I think it hasn't been done before is it doesn't benefit leadership. It benefits the organization and not the leadership. It helps them to scramble us all the time, and it helps them to throw us chaotic curveballs,” Houlahan told NOTUS.

Even if her party wins the majority in November, Houlahan has set her expectations quite low.

“Regardless of who's in charge, I'm sad to think or believe that it probably won't be a heck of a lot better, which is why most people at this point are trying to just try to make it incrementally better,” she told NOTUS.

Some proposals dealt with making the House more ethical and transparent to constituents, several of which have already received media attention:

  • Several Republicans and Democrats called for a ban on lawmakers trading individual stocks, an issue that various House speakers have stumbled over in recent years.
  • Several lawmakers called for formal bans against members and staff placing wagers on prediction markets like Kalshi, behavior that has led to insider-trading investigations. 
  • Several lawmakers requested rules that would allow expectant and new parents to cast their votes by proxy to be a more family-friendly House, a proposal that House Speaker Mike Johnson has blocked.
  • Republicans and Democrats requested a new provision that would allow bill introductions to have multiple lead sponsors, instead of the current practice of just one.
  • Rep. Kevin Kiley, the only House independent, asked to change the rules to allow members who are elected as independents to receive committee assignments without caucusing with either party. 


These modest proposals often serve as attempts to more broadly shift the operations of the House, with younger Democrats highlighting how hard it is for a young woman to run for Congress if she wants to raise a family.

“Honestly, this place doesn’t really work for younger people,” said Democratic Rep. Sara Jacobs, 37, who talked about freezing her eggs to try to time when she gets pregnant.

Democratic Rep. Brittany Pettersen, 44, explained how she repeatedly had to fly from Denver to Washington last year with her newborn, Samuel, during very close-margin votes on major legislation.

Before he turned 6 months old, Samuel had been on 24 flights.

“This place doesn’t have to work this way,” Pettersen said.

The congressional calendar drew the most ire from both sides of the aisle.

Rank-and-file lawmakers complain that they spend way too much time on airplanes darting back and forth from their districts to Washington, leaving little time to be in the Capitol debating and shaping actual legislation.

For more than 15 years, the model month in the House has been three weeks in session and one week at home. Each week in Washington usually starts Monday evening and ends Thursday morning. That’s just two full days a week in session and two days a week traveling through airports or train stations.

Fine told Reps. Virginia Foxx and Jim McGovern, the Republican and Democratic committee leaders who have more than 50 years of combined congressional experience, that he might have a magical formula.

Commit to a full week or two in a row in Washington, creating at least four full days a week in committees and voting, followed by a corresponding number of weeks in their districts, he suggested.

“I’ve done the math on this,” Fine, the newest member to testify, said. “If we actually did this — a week here and a week home — we would actually spend more time working in Washington, we would spend more time working in our districts, and we would spend less time sitting on airplanes.”

Foxx responded to the schedule and travel complaints by recalling what her mentor told her when she won her first House race in 2004: “The worst part of this job is the travel.”

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver served as the lead Democratic co-sponsor on a prominent housing bill that was signed into law earlier this year, with Republican Rep. Mike Flood officially labeled the lead sponsor. Cleaver, an 11-term member, thinks younger lawmakers would benefit if multiple bill sponsors could be listed, which could encourage more bipartisan efforts.

“So it will automatically create alliances that don't exist now,” Cleaver told NOTUS after his testimony.

Some lawmakers talked about truly transformational changes, such as implementing stricter controls on the revolving door that sends many members to lobbying firms upon retirement and banning gerrymandering to create politically safe districts.

But, for now, most lawmakers would settle for some basic changes like real training for dealing with classified information.

“I was shocked and have been shocked for four years now,” Kiggans told the committee.

Houlahan, who also serves on the Armed Services Committee and other informal groups dealing with national security, said she would settle for a balanced schedule that allowed her to attend and participate in these meetings.

“We're not stupid. We can figure this out. We just don't even try,” she told NOTUS.

entries.title: As Trump Eyes D.C. Golf Course, Patrons Putt in Purgatory
entries.summary: Thursday’s hearing offered no insight on when the course might close for Trump’s renovation
entries.content:
On the morning it was supposed to shut down, East Potomac Golf Links woke up just as it had for generations. Bicycles buzzed to the north. Jets growled to the south. The bleary-eyed toted their clubs — clank, clank, clank. The first golfer walked into the pro shop at 7:01 a.m.

“We’re still here?” Sito Pantoja said.

“We’re still here!” replied a beloved clubhouse attendant known as “Country.”

Pantoja, a retiree from the suburbs, felt terrible for the employees. They’d been living in purgatory since last winter, when the president greenlit a plan to dump the dirt from his demolition of the White House’s East Wing in the nearby park — and then use that dirt to renovate the golf course.

Months of politicking, protests and lawyering had led to Sept. 1 — the day President Donald Trump had said work would begin to turn the 300-acre municipal complex into a “championship” course capable of hosting professional tournaments. But when Pantoja got out of his car, he saw no blockades. He saw no bulldozers. He paid $29 and turned to head for the tee box.

“You’re gonna let this guy play here?” a friend joked, and the pro shop fell into a familiar rhythm.
DSC06747 copy.jpg (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)For the rest of the week, in came a procession of polo shirts — fuzzy white, polyester black and every shade of the sweat-stained rainbow. They asked the clubhouse attendants how many more trees had been chopped down (dunno) and when they’d close for real (ditto). They asked whether they could book tee times for next week (sure can) and how the staff was holding up (“Can’t complain,” Country said). They asked for updates on the lawsuit to block the renovations (the Trump administration told a judge Thursday that 150 trees were recently removed for routine maintenance, not because major construction was imminent). “We’re still here!” attendants said over and over, and they told the golfers that it’d stay that way until they heard otherwise from the National Park Service.

Golfers seethed. They knew this precarity was not unique in Trump’s America, that they were just a few angry people in a nation that largely disapproved of how far he’d gone to reshape the capital in his own image. But it was still infuriating to think about the president, with all his other problems, paying such close attention to their little oasis. Last month, New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman estimated that Trump devotes 70% of his mental energy to his legacy projects, such as a triumphal arch, a new White House ballroom and renaming the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

“He has no plan,” one man said.

“People can’t even buy gas,” said another.

“He just got his goddamn ballroom,” announced a man in a straw hat, holding up his phone to show everyone the Supreme Court had voted, 5-4, to clear the way for construction at the White House to continue. “He’s gonna get the Kennedy Center. This is next.”
DSC06244 copy 2.jpg (6251x4167, AR: 1.50)Mark Ellmore, another retiree, walked into the pro shop. He liked what Trump was doing. He came here all the time, sometimes just to walk around, and the course looked to him like it could use a little love. In his mind, the people who opposed the renovation were rich, old, white “humanists” who wanted the government to subsidize their golf. But today wasn’t the day to make that case, so he fist-bumped the clubhouse attendant and walked out.

The only appearance from the National Park Service was when a man in an official black polo stopped by to order lunch from the course grill.

Outside, the saws got closer to the clubhouse. RTEC Treecare had been chopping for a week and installed a pop-up notice on its website. “To Concerned Citizens,” it began, before going on to say it had proudly worked for the federal government for 30 years “across four presidential administrations.” One sentence was in bold: RTEC Treecare has not removed any cherry trees.

Inside, the pro shop was barren. Empty shelves. Blank slatwalls. Not even a box of golf balls.

“This is so sad,” a gray-haired woman said.

“We’re staying strong,” Country replied.

It went on like that until the shadows ate the greens. But even in near-total darkness, golfers kept swinging, not knowing when it would really end. And then, on Wednesday morning, the golf course woke up again. Bicycles. Jets. Clank, clank, clank. And on Thursday, at 7:01 a.m., Sito Pantoja, the retiree from the suburbs, stood at the first tee box with his friends, ready to keep swinging.

entries.title: Crashing the Party
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Sept. 4, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

A happy birthday to D.C.’s Department of For-Hire Vehicles, which celebrated turning 10 yesterday with a celebration at MLK Memorial Library. It was a joyful occasion, celebrating D.C.’s taxicab drivers with a live band, canapés and an awards ceremony.

But the party masked a sober reality. The industry faces a watershed moment, as autonomous vehicles could be permitted to operate in the city this fall.

“Hell no, Waymo!” chanted one attendee, disability advocate Heidi Case, as DFHV Director Jonathan Rogers took the stage for a speech.

“We’ll talk about Waymo, Heidi,” Rogers replied. “Because that’s one of the themes: We’ve had a lot of change over the past 10 years, and there’s a lot more coming. We’ll handle it together.”

DFHV was created to meet a specific moment, Rogers said. Ten years ago, the agency was charged with modernizing the city’s taxicabs and regulating rideshare services Uber and Lyft, which had recently made their entry into D.C. with few guardrails. The decade since has seen the number of active cabs on the street drop from 8,000-10,000 to around 1,400, Rogers previously told NOTUS.

“We’re in another one of those moments, where a lot is changing again because technology is not slowing down,” Rogers said.

Drivers are anxious about their livelihoods. Abeba Berhe, who’s been driving a wheelchair-accessible cab in D.C. and Virginia for 20 years, told NOTUS she thinks the entry of autonomous vehicles would be a “disaster” for her industry.

“Driver jobs are getting disappeared. … Our job income [has] shrunk,” Berhe said, adding that she already has trouble making credit card payments every month.

There will always be a role for the “human element” of for-hire vehicles, Rogers told NOTUS. The D.C. Council, including Janeese Lewis George, has expressed concern about workforce impacts and accessibility, he said.

“There’s always been disruption and new competition,” Rogers said. “There are things that humans are able to do as a driver, as an assistant in a vehicle, that AVs are not likely to do any time in the near future.”





DEEP DIVE

An update on East Potomac Park: At a hearing Thursday, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes emphasized that she is “not the Lorax”: She does not, in fact, speak for the trees.

About 150 of them have come down at East Potomac in recent days, a removal campaign that the government called “routine maintenance” but that raised alarm with the public. NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad reports that Reyes said Thursday she has received several angry calls, including one advocating for her disbarment if she did not stop the tree removal.

Although she previously asked the government to notify her before cutting down more than 10 trees, Reyes said that did not apply to maintenance and she had no issues with last week’s work.

An amended complaint is expected to be filed by the plaintiffs — preservationists seeking to block the park’s renovation — by Sept. 12. Reyes declined to rule on the DOJ’s recent motion to dismiss the case until she receives that complaint.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Trump arch AP - 26185088891653 (6755x4503, AR: 1.50)
President Donald Trump’s plan to construct a 250-foot arch in D.C. will move forward, with excavation work starting in the next two weeks, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced Thursday. NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports that the project, which was displayed in miniature at the Great American State Fair this summer, will be located near Arlington National Cemetery. A lawsuit challenging its construction is still pending in the U.S. District Court for D.C.

Federal prosecutors are accusing Ward 8 council member Trayon White of jury tampering in the wake of a video posted on Instagram this week where he spoke about his upcoming trial on federal bribery charges and addressed the jury selection process, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports. Prosecutors have asked a judge to admonish White, while White’s defense team says he “expressed nothing unlawful.”

A pied-à-terre tax for D.C.? Council Chair Phil Mendelson has scheduled an Oct. 16 public hearing where lawmakers will hear testimony and debate possible revenue-raising options, ranging from a hike in capital gains taxes to new levies on second homes. With D.C.’s economy souring in the wake of sweeping federal layoffs, city revenue has dried up and lawmakers are facing a large budget deficit in the year to come.

Not a state, but still quite fair. The D.C. State Fair returns Sunday with “art, agriculture, and the culinary arts.” It’ll take place at Anthem Row (800 K St. NW) from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.





FROM VIRGINIA

Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam has learned his phone calls with state Sen. Louise Lucas were monitored by the FBI and DOJ as part of a broader investigation into Lucas, Subramanyam said in a statement Thursday. Lucas’s calls with two journalists were also monitored, Virginia Scope reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Maryland has lost more than $800 million by failing to collect tolls and penalties that drivers owed, The Washington Post reports.

A budding dispute: The University of Maryland is threatening legal action against a cannabis company in Colorado over its name: “Terps USA,” WTOP reports.





METRO MOMENTS

Raising her son in D.C., Kainaz Amaria — NOTUS’ senior editor of visual storytelling — didn’t get a sense that kids are growing up with a shared story. Many schools have specialized curriculums these days, so there is little that is universal about how and what our kids learn. But since 2016, her son and nearly 100,000 other children across the District have had something in common: a gift in the mail every month from “The Book Lady,” Dolly Parton, Kainaz writes in NOTUS Perspectives.

We want to hear from you: Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.

In recent years, Thomas Boswell has found the Nationals to be almost unwatchable. So, Boswell writes, it is a testament to Washington’s new regime that the team is still entertaining at this point in the season. As long as there are some ups with the downs, the Nats retain their power to please.

Meanwhile, outfielder Daylen Lile is in the middle of a loud, elongated “up” of an up-and-down season for the Nationals. NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty writes that his recent stretch is a reason to believe Lile could be a key part of the next winning core in Washington. But, as with many baseball players, that will come down to whether Lile, an unforgiving perfectionist, can quiet the negative thoughts in his head.

entries.title: Early Departure
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Nice to briefly see you, Congress. Pentagon accused of eating off another agency’s plate. Life at the East Potomac Golf Links. And: Epstein survivors don’t feel heard at the new DOJ. 

Programming note No. 1: We’ll be off for Labor Day — probably laboring over a grill or buying a new air fryer the ads tell us we need — but back in your inbox Tuesday morning.

Programming note No. 2: Last chance to take our five-minute survey! Help us make a better NOTUS newsletter.





THE LATEST

What did we learn in Congress this week? America’s lawmakers came back to D.C. for a few days after their August break. It was … dramatic. And short! The last two weeks of House votes this month were hastily canceled, leaving only one week to try to legislate before the midterms. (The Senate treks in Sept. 14 and will be around until Oct. 1.) We asked NOTUS’ crack team of Hill lurkers observers what they took away from it all.

The birth of a new House rebellion and the end of an old one. Footage of Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern (D-Massachusetts) physically turning his back on Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Washington state), after she and Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) helped bail out Republicans, was more than just the traditional Democratic Disarray, NOTUS’ Paul Kane tells us. It could be a passing of the torch from one tough-to-manage majority to another.

“We (possibly) saw the last gasps of the Tea Party uprising that began in 2010 and gained steam when the Freedom Caucus flexed its power in the late 2010s and now stumbled into political reckoning this spring and summer after a series of defeats,” Paul told us.

More of PK’s wisdom: “A week that was supposed to turn into fallout and recriminations amid Republican failure turned into shock and awe among Democrats at the mini-rebellion, foreshadowing that should they win the majority and take charge next year, the next-generation leadership team will face a lot more difficulty uniting their caucus than their octogenarian predecessors had a few years ago.”

What does it means for the rest of the year? Democrats have the traditional momentum of the out-of-power party in the midterms this cycle, bolstered by a public increasingly unhappy with Donald Trump. But very soon they may find they are the dogs who finally caught the car — centrists like Gluesenkamp Perez doing everything they can to stand apart from the surging socialist wing of the party (and vice versa) does not bode well for the kind of unity Democrats will need to turn a potential protest-vote midterm win into a chance to rebuild their shattered public image.

Mike Johnson is rattled. “He’s been extra spicy/cranky this week,” observed NOTUS’ Igor Bobic. Can you blame him? Asked whether he should be held accountable for his claims that the Iran war would end quickly by CNN’s Manu Raju, Johnson called it “one of the stupidest questions” the reporter’s ever asked him. “I have nothing to do with the prosecution of a war across the globe,” Johnson said.

What this means for the rest of the year. If Johnson doesn’t have a better answer for the White House policy moves bedeviling Republicans in public polling, it’s hard to believe his candidates will either.

Looking past the election, there’s a growing number of lawmakers thinking about weeks like this one and saying something fundamental has to change. Paul’s latest column dives into all the bipartisan ideas to reform how Congress works. Like, say, mandatory training on how to handle classified materials, or maybe formally barring members and staff from using prediction markets in an attempt to return some credibility to the Capitol. Let’s see how that goes.

Open tabs: GOP lawmaker gives expected timeline for McConnell’s return (CNN) | Tucker Carlson: “I wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers at gun point.” (X) | Pentagon temporarily rescinds guidance on testosterone screening for US troops (Reuters)





From the Pentagon


Scoop: DOD sought access to NIH’s money, Democrat says. Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement to NOTUS’ Joe Gould that she found evidence the Pentagon tried to get its hands on billions of dollars appropriated for biomedical research. DeLauro described what transpired as a Pentagon “attempt” and that it was not immediately clear how much money the department was seeking, where within the DOD it would go or what it would pay for. She accused the Pentagon of effectively rifling through the government’s couch cushions to find money to pay for the ongoing Iran war and other cash-flow challenges.

The National Institutes of Health said it and the Defense Department had explored ways to collaborate on therapeutics, diagnostics and personal protective equipment to defend against infectious diseases. “NIH enters into partnerships with numerous government agencies,” a spokesperson said.





THE BIG ONE

Justice deferred: Hope rose among some victims of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein when survivors finally got a meeting with Todd Blanche at the Justice Department’s headquarters in July. But that hope has now plummeted after weeks of inaction and lack of communication, the survivors told NOTUS’ Derek Hawkins. And it’s reinforced their belief that the Blanche-led department has no intention of pursuing the issues they brought to him.

“There’s just not an interest,” Annie Farmer, one of the survivors, said in an interview with Derek. “They want to move on and turn the page.”

For its part, the DOJ declined to answer questions about its interactions with survivors. Instead, in an unsigned email, the department told NOTUS: “We have responded to all requests for meetings w/ victims and/or their advocates.”





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

On Tuesday, New Hampshire voters will decide whether Scott Brown gets another shot at being a senator. At NOTUS Perspectives, journalist Bill Donahue, who joined him on the campaign trail, argues that Brown embodies the fraught position of Republicans in 2026: locked in a destructive embrace of Trump with no real way out.

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Sports desk: Daylen Lile, Nationals Cornerstone? By Jesse Dougherty





NEW ON NOTUS

“We’re still here!” That was the refrain from duffers playing through at the East Potomac Golf Links this week, the one that was supposed to mark the closure of the federally run D.C. public course Trump wants to demolish and rebuild as PGA worthy. NOTUS’ Sam Fortier talked to the golfers and the staff as they sounded off on the renovation project currently tied up in court and considered their role in the president’s grand plans to leave his mark on their city.

entries.title: Iran War Widow Who Posted About ‘Missing’ Benefits Says Her Case Is Resolved
entries.summary: Libby Klinner said the incident reflects how difficult it can be for grieving families to navigate government processes.
entries.content:
The Gold Star widow of an Air Force service member who died in support of the ongoing U.S. war with Iran said in a statement Thursday that the Defense Department had completed its review of her headline-grabbing benefits case.

The case of Libby Klinner, the wife of Maj. John A. Klinner, who was one of six service members killed when an aircraft crashed in Iraq during a refueling mission on March 12, spread this week after she claimed on Instagram that she was informed she could not receive certain combat-related benefits because Congress had not officially declared the military operations in Iran a war.

But after a review of her case, an Air Force spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement that officials have confirmed all eligible combat-pay-related benefits, including imminent-danger pay, hostile-fire pay and combat-zone tax-exclusion benefits, were “included in the arrears of pay [Klinner] has already received.”

She confirmed the findings in a statement to CNN on Thursday evening.

“That was the information I shared publicly at the time,” Klinner said. “As the story spread, however, it created the impression that our family’s military benefits had been broadly denied or withheld, which was not the case.”

Klinner said the Pentagon has since reviewed her case and confirmed her family had received all of its benefits, adding she was “grateful to everyone who helped bring clarity and resolution to this deeply personal matter.” Klinner said the experience reflects “how difficult it can be for a grieving family to navigate classifications, terminology and government processes at the very moment we are least equipped to do so.”

“No Gold Star family should have to become an expert in government language to understand what they are entitled to,” she said.

Combat-zone tax-exclusion benefits are based on geographic location and effective dates, according to the pay tables posted to the Pentagon’s Defense Finance and Accounting Service website. Imminent-danger pay is likewise determined by select locations, including various areas throughout the Middle East, and whether the operation was “directed by President of the United States,” the website says.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters during a briefing Thursday that the Trump administration would directly connect with Klinner to ensure she receives all of her benefits.

“My message to her would be: We love you, we're grateful for the sacrifice and we very much take very seriously our commitment to get you what you need to get,” Vance said.

entries.title: Watchdog Report Says Chavez-DeRemer Oversaw a ‘Toxic’ Workplace
entries.summary: The former Labor Secretary stepped down following multiple allegations of inappropriate behavior while in office.
entries.content:
Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer oversaw a “toxic, intimidating and humiliating” workplace and repeatedly violated department policy, according to an internal watchdog report released Thursday evening.

The report contains testimony from dozens of witnesses who say Chavez-DeRemer failed to prevent persistent harassment, regularly drank alcohol on the job and spent federal money on personal travel.

The 44-page report comes several months after Chavez-DeRemer resigned in April following multiple allegations of inappropriate behavior. She was the third Cabinet official under President Donald Trump’s second term to step down and was scheduled to be interviewed by agency Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito’s office when she resigned.

D’Esposito found that Chavez-DeRemer was involved in an "unprofessional relationship” with a member of her security team, but did not “obtain sufficient direct evidence to establish that the relationship was romantic or sexual.”

The report describes one incident in which Chavez-DeRemer visited a strip club with the security agent during a personal trip to her home state of Oregon. The then-secretary asked a driver to go inside with them and requested he give money to a semi-nude performer. When the driver resisted, the security agent told the driver to comply and later to keep quiet about the encounter.

Witnesses cited in the report also said Chavez-DeRemer publicly discussed employee performance, and sent Labor Department employees to perform tasks at her home, including laundry and organizing her closet. The report found that Chavez-DeRemer “regularly drank alcohol in [her] study during official duty hours,” and when other employees attending meetings declined alcohol, she and others “pressured them to participate or ridiculed them for abstaining.”

Chavez-DeRemer’s nationwide listening tour, called “America at Work,” often centered around destinations where the secretary had friends or family, according to the report. Witnesses said she required stops to be within one hour of a commercial airport and limited site visits to 60 to 90 minutes.

Chavez-DeRemer has publicly disputed the allegations through an agency spokeswoman but did not immediately return a request for comment from NOTUS.

Following her departure, Chavez-DeRemer launched a Republican-aligned political action committee, the American Workers First PAC.

entries.title: U.S. Job Market Rebounds in Surprising Fashion While Unemployment Stays Flat
entries.summary: Revisions also added 55,000 jobs to June and July payrolls.
entries.content:
By Paul Wiseman

The U.S. job market rebounded in August as employers added a surprising 162,000 jobs. The unemployment stayed at a low 4.1%.



Revisions added 55,000 jobs to June and July payrolls.



Hiring has been up and down this year, two months before midterm elections and at a time when voters are unhappy about the economy and the high cost of living in particular.



Companies are contending with a shortage of workers — the result of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and the retirement of baby boomers — and some are responding by using technology for tasks that human beings used to do.



But employers have been relucutant to let go of the staff they have, so most Americans enjoy unusual job security and unemployment is low.

entries.title: HHS Cancels Infant Mortality, Postpartum Grants to Focus on Sperm Counts, ED
entries.summary: Officials at the Office of Minority Health told grantees that they’re prioritizing “root causes” of infertility and promoting exercise.
entries.content:
The Health Department’s office to improve the health of minorities has abruptly terminated more than half its existing grants, saying they didn’t focus on the Trump administration’s new priorities of addressing infertility and encouraging exercise.

Some grantees provided cancer screenings or postpartum home visits. Others worked to reduce first-responder suicide or decrease obesity among Native American youth. All of the funds came from the Office of Minority Health, which the administration tried to shutter last year.

Administration officials wrote to grantees that going forward, awards should directly advance “reducing overmedicalization in health care by addressing the root causes of infertility” including hormonal imbalances, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, low sperm count, low testosterone levels and erectile dysfunction as root causes.

Grants should also support programs that promote “regular physical activity and exercise,” according to the Aug. 25 letters obtained by NOTUS.

The termination letters were sent to 16 county, state and nonprofit grantees, according to a list from a source familiar with the agency’s decision and an online database. The 16 grants totalled $38 million over four years. The grantees had received the first two years of funding.

Several grantees told NOTUS they had been fully expecting to receive their third funding installment for the four-year grants and were caught entirely by surprise. They’d worried last year, when President Donald Trump’s budget proposed cutting Office of Minority Health grants by 40%, but thought their funding was safe after that never transpired.

“We thought we had weathered the storm,” said Christopher Joseph, the executive director of EngageWell, which was administering a grant awarded to Brooklyn-based nonprofit Housing Works.

Joseph said his group was using its grant to help hypertension patients monitor their blood pressure from home and deliver boxes of fresh produce and eggs to 150 New Yorkers every other week as part of a program called “Food as Medicine.”

He’d assumed the food-delivery program would be safe from cuts, because it dovetails with the focus on preventive health in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

“When MAHA came about we thought great, this aligns with their priorities,” Joseph said.

Many of the termination letters contained virtually identical language. They said the awards being canceled no longer advance “current agency priorities.”

The letters were signed by Eric West, acting chief grants officer at the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, and Mahyar Mofidi, deputy assistant secretary for minority health.

The administration wrote to several grantees working on maternal health that while “maternal and infant health are important issues,” their work “does not advance minority health with regards to OMH’s current priority areas.”

One of those grantees, the Denver-based nonprofit Illuminate Colorado, sends nurses to the homes of minority women in the days after they give birth, checking to make sure they’re able to care for themselves and their newborns.

“It was news to us that maternal and infant fatality prevention wasn’t a priority,” said the group’s co-executive director Jillian Fabricius.

The Department of Health and Human Services didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The cuts are just the latest example of grants abruptly terminated by the Trump administration as it seeks to put its own stamp on the aid and research being funded by the federal government. Over the summer it canceled 150 awards funding health delivery research and previously delayed hundreds of millions of dollars in grants for additional political review.

Under the Biden administration, the Office of Minority Health funded dozens of grants every year. Now the agency’s website lists only two funding opportunities for fiscal year 2026, one for lupus research and the other to address chronic disease among Native Americans.

The office was created under President Ronald Reagan. Its grant awards surged during President Joe Biden’s first year but last year declined back to 2019 levels. The Trump administration appears to be further slashing funding; in addition to the 16 canceled grants, 13 that were funded last year appear to be unfunded this year, according to a public database.

Last year, Kennedy tried to eliminate the Office of Minority Health entirely as he reorganized the department and shed around 20,000 employees, though Congress ultimately declined to go along with the plan.

Trump has continued to target minority-focused offices within HHS: In his fiscal 2027 budget, he proposed eliminating the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities, zeroing out the Minority HIV/AIDS office and slashing the Office of Minority Health funding by 40%.

One grantee, the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, said its program to reduce infant and maternal mortality among Black families in the Arkansas Delta will likely end without the grant.

Spokesperson Leslie Taylor said she was not sure why the grant was canceled, though she said "it's certainly a big issue in our state considering we're number one in the country,” referring to the high infant and maternal mortality rates in Arkansas.

Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colorado), the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, asked the administration to explain the grant terminations and its new funding priorities.

“It is shocking that OMH under any leadership would prioritize erectile dysfunction over the health and wellbeing of infants and new mothers, yet that is precisely what you are doing,” she wrote Thursday to Brian Christine, the assistant secretary for health.

entries.title: An Ex-Ecuadorian Official Said He Was in Political Danger. The U.S. Deported Him.
entries.summary: José Serrano Salgado fled to Miami when the South American country swung from left to right politically.
entries.content:
Last Friday, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents hauled José Serrano Salgado onto a poshly decorated jet in South Florida bound for Ecuador — even though there had been a judge’s order in May temporarily pausing his deportation for fear of torture back home.

That torture is what a source told NOTUS is happening to him now. Ecuadorian jailers are now smashing his fingernails, denying him food and subjecting him to loud and unceasing noise, according to a person who got a phone call Monday about Serrano’s situation.

A flight manifest obtained by NOTUS shows that Serrano — once a top Ecuadorian security official — was the lone deportee on the flight aboard a Challenger 350 owned by the self-described “luxury private jet charter” Reliance Jets.

Serrano, a former interior minister in the old leftist administration who ended up in the United States after a rightward political swing in the country, was formally charged with murder last year by the Ecuadorian attorney general’s office on allegations he was the mastermind behind a political assassination.

Juan Pablo Segura, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for Western Hemisphere affairs, posted a statement on X that claimed Serrano was “wanted by INTERPOL” and “will now face justice in Ecuador.” However, Serrano is not among the 6,417 public “red notices” listed by INTERPOL.

Instead, he was sent back through the immigration system. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Serrano was arrested and detained because he was illegally in the country, and the U.S. told a federal judge he was removed pursuant to a final administrative order.

The high-profile ICE deportation marks the latest step in the increasingly cozy martial relationship between the United States and Ecuador, which includes an expanding war against drug cartels and the creation of a southbound deportation pipeline.

Segura, in his post, wrote that under President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, “the United States will never again be a safe haven for foreign criminals and thugs” and put the emoji flags for the two countries side by side.

But that partnership has raised human rights concerns. That includes the American military’s extrajudicial killings of sailors at sea accused of drug-running without public presentation of evidence, and the decision to make the dangerous Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil the final stop for U.S. deportees who aren’t even from that country, as NOTUS reporting on the ground showed.

Serrano’s deportation has all the markings of a formal extradition on criminal charges but without the typical legal assurances that a prisoner will be treated fairly.

His lawyers raced to file an emergency petition before the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals to keep him from being rushed to Ecuador, but Serrano was still removed. Miami immigration judge Romy Lerner on May 13 had granted him a “deferral of removal under the Convention Against Torture.”

That ruling previously halted what ICE itself admitted would have been a mistaken deportation back in June, as laid out in court filings related to Serrano’s habeas corpus lawsuit in his monthslong attempt to be released while in the United States. 

According to that court docket, which remains largely inaccessible to the public, the Justice Department notified the judge on Monday that ICE had “executed” a warrant of removal. U.S. District Judge K. Michael Moore dismissed the lawsuit on Wednesday, noting that Serrano had already been deported “pursuant to a final administrative order” — however, it’s unclear when that order was filed or why.

It’s also unclear who paid for the private jet that took Serrano from the Miami suburbs to Guayaquil, because Reliance Jets has not been known to be an ICE contractor. (The charter company did not respond to NOTUS questions sent Wednesday.)

Serrano was once president of Ecuador’s legislative branch. In 2016, he traveled to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration’s headquarters to personally receive an award for “strong leadership” in the international fight against narco-traffickers.

But then the country swung from left to right, and the new administration pulled his security detail. He fled to Miami in 2021. And it’s while living there that he was accused of helping orchestrate the 2023 assassination of an Ecuadorian presidential candidate.

President Daniel Noboa, the young conservative president of Ecuador whose militant approach to crime has drawn comparisons to the right-wing Salvadoran head of state Nayib Bukele, posted pictures of Serrano being escorted into a prison cell by masked police.

https://x.com/DanielNoboaOk/status/2093742485486903307
“Hecho,” he wrote, the Spanish equivalent of simply stating, “done.”

The criminal investigation has captivated the South American nation, as a political conspiracy with sprawling tentacles whose fallout is still being felt today.

The ultimate conclusion of that investigation could align neatly with the Trump administration’s hard-right approach to international relations, as it presents an opportunity to target leftist former President Rafael Correa and his associates — and expand conservative U.S. influence in South America by striking a blow to the broader Chavista political movement in the region.

The current Ecuadorian president indicated as much in a post on X that called Serrano the “new guest” at El Encuentro, a maximum-security prison modeled after El Salvador’s notorious CECOT.

“Now it’s your turn,” Noboa publicly warned Correa, who now lives in exile in Belgium.

https://x.com/DanielNoboaOk/status/2093489752464859513
There are already signs that the Trump administration is poised to nudge the Ecuadorian investigation forward. Last year, federal agents, an hour before dawn, raided the Miami home of Xavier Jordan, an Ecuadorian businessman whom Ecuadorian investigators have tied to the assassination plot.

Jordan sued the anti-corruption politician Fernando Villavicencio for defamation in Miami-Dade County in 2023, in a complaint that said he had been falsely accused of ties to a narco-financier named Leandro Norero.

This week, Jordan told NOTUS how “special tactical teams” and officials from the Department of Justice, FBI, ICE and even the State Department entered his home, where two young children were present, and confiscated documents he collected that he said “alleged corruption involving Ecuadorian government officials.”

“They did not ask me about my immigration status. I believe they realized that they had been misled by false information provided by the Ecuadorian government and that disproportionate force had been used to conduct the raid,” he said.

Jordan said he never communicated with Norero, who is now dead.

In some ways, the United States has been a driving force from the start of the investigation into the plot to kill Villavicencio, a journalist-turned-legislator who exposed the relationships between narco-traffickers and high-ranking government officials.

Villavicencio was fatally shot by contracted Colombian sicarios days before the initial round of presidential elections in 2023. The Ecuadorian government managed to catch six members of the seven-person hit team and immediately requested American assistance.

According to two people familiar with the investigation who spoke to NOTUS on condition of anonymity, the FBI helped the Ecuadorian National Police unlock almost 100 seized phones, interviewed every member of the Colombian death squad and recorded one of them giving a detailed confession that claimed the authors of the plot ran straight to the highest levels of the ousted Correa government.

After that confession, the FBI and U.S. embassy urgently recommended multiple times that the assassins be transferred from the jail where they were being held — but those requests were ignored and all the men were strangled to death, these sources told NOTUS.

The investigation, dubbed “Metástasis,” has become Ecuador’s largest ever anti-corruption case to reveal links between top government officials and drug traffickers.

Serrano vehemently denies his involvement and claims that his name appears nowhere in the massive trove of evidence uncovered by investigators. But he was nonetheless formally charged with murder last year by the Ecuadorian attorney general’s office, which alleged he was the mastermind behind the political assassination of Villavicencio.

Serrano’s case portends the strengthening of U.S.-Ecuador security ties. President Noboa’s requests that the United States arrest Serrano in Miami went ignored for years. But just days after then-Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem met with Noboa in Ecuador in July, he was arrested by four ICE agents as he neared his mailbox outside his Miami home, according to a source who knows about the encounter who requested to remain anonymous fearing political reprisals.

Serrano stayed in ICE detention at Miami’s Krome North Service Processing Center for most of his yearlong detention, court records show. A source told NOTUS Serrano lost approximately 25 pounds and saw his prediabetes progress into full-blown diabetes.

The Ecuadorian embassy did not respond to NOTUS questions about how Serrano’s prisoner transfer was arranged nor offer an update on his current condition.

The Department of Homeland Security did not answer NOTUS questions about what legal authority permitted Serrano’s deportation, nor why the U.S. chose to deport him rather than criminally charge him here if he did indeed plot a murder while living on U.S. soil.

Instead, the department sent a statement noting that there was no federal court order barring the government from deporting Serrano: “The Department of Homeland Security does not conduct immigration enforcement on behalf of foreign political interests, nor does it target individuals for protected political speech. What makes someone a target of ICE is being in the country illegally.”

entries.summary: A planning commission voted to transfer jurisdiction of the land, the first step in giving the city authority over it.
entries.content:
The District’s redevelopment plan for the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium campus is one step closer to fruition after a federal planning commission approved the transfer Thursday of the D.C. Armory to local control.

The National Capital Planning Commission voted to transfer jurisdiction of the 9.4 acres to D.C., the first step in giving the local government authority over the land. The transfer still has to be approved by the mayor, the D.C. Council and Congress.

The D.C. Armory, headquarters of the D.C. National Guard, is included in the District’s drafted master plan as a space to be “considered in concert with” the development of the Commanders’ stadium and surrounding recreation areas. Similar to the rest of the RFK site, the federal government will retain ownership of the property, but the District will be in charge of maintaining and redeveloping it.

Plans for the site remain up in the air. The RFK site plan recommends the land be used for commercial and residential development, but the transfer agreement does not approve the demolition of the Armory building. A spokesperson at the RFK Project Management Office said the District “has not made a final determination about the future use of the DC Armory site” and that any future use will require planning and review.

Though the Armory will remain standing, it will likely no longer be home to the D.C. National Guard, which is looking for a new headquarters site. Spokesperson Arthur Wright said the redevelopment of the RFK campus will affect the Guard’s mission capabilities, thus necessitating the move. The Guard hasn’t made any final decisions but is primarily considering an 80-acre patch of land at the Armed Forces Retirement Home in Northwest D.C.

“This effort is designed to be a strategic investment in our national security, ensuring our soldiers and airmen have the state-of-the-art facilities they need to respond to any crisis,” he said. “We are committed to working closely with our partners in the D.C. government and the local community throughout this process.”

entries.title: ‘Fetterman Is a Disgrace,’ Democrats Say After Bombshell Article
entries.summary: The piece cites more than a dozen of Fetterman’s former aides and colleagues who accuse the Pennsylvania senator of shirking his congressional duties.
entries.content:
Sen. John Fetterman was criticized by his Democratic peers Friday morning after a cutting Wall Street Journal article showed him shirking his committee duties, dodging face time with constituents and complaining about attending a set of police funerals.

Other members of the Pennsylvania delegation denounced the behavior, with some promising to oust Fetterman if he decides to run for reelection in 2028.

“John Fetterman is a disgrace,” Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pennsylvania) wrote on X. “Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job.”

Once touted by progressives as a hoodie-wearing populist darling, Fetterman’s popularity with Democrats has soured this year, particularly after he joined Republicans on Iran war powers votes and indicated he could leave the party if leadership makes opposition to Israel central to its platform.

The Journal report cited more than a dozen of Fetterman’s former staffers and colleagues, as well as verified internal texts in which the senator demonstrated a lack of interest in participating in the basic duties associated with his position.

Ex-staffers told the newspaper he chose conservative media hits and pro-Israel activism over routine Senate work. During one stretch, the senator reportedly skipped 11 of 12 full hearings between a handful of board appointments, and later instructed his staff to ensure he was marked “present” at hearings even when he stayed for a minute or less.

Fetterman’s former chief of staff, Adam Jentleson, said on X that the senator’s aides “apparently find themselves horrified at Fetterman’s behavior,” more than two years after Jentleson left his post.

“Between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty. He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028,” Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pennsylvania) wrote Friday morning on X.

The article highlighted additional concerns about his interactions with local constituents: In June, three paralyzed military veterans traveled from rural Pennsylvania to meet with Fetterman about health care legislation. The senator canceled on them, instructing staff to say he had a stomach bug, before appearing for a live interview on Fox News that day. And last September, he reportedly dismissed children's hospital officials who were visiting D.C. to discuss vaccines and Medicaid cuts, quipping that they just wanted "free trips” to the capital.

When Pennsylvania state Rep. Liz Hanbidge traveled to Washington for a scheduled meeting on homelessness and working-class issues, Fetterman skipped it for a meeting with former NCAA basketball coach and pro-Israel advocate Bruce Pearl.

Internal communications showed that Fetterman refused to attend a three-hour funeral for fallen local police officers in Pennsylvania, declaring the length of the service a "nonstarter."

Former Rep. Conor Lamb, who lost to Fetterman by over 30 percentage points in the 2022 Senate primary and could launch a new campaign for 2028, said the senator should submit his resignation papers.


“John, if there is a decent bone left in your body, just quit. It’s an insult to decent people in our state for you to treat them and the office this way,” he wrote on X.


Fetterman had already isolated himself from most party allies by the time President Donald Trump retook office.

He took a meeting with Trump at Mar-a-lago in January 2025 before his inauguration. And in March 2025, when aides informed him that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was organizing a special conference call for Democrats, Fetterman wrote in texts, “I truly don’t care,” the Journal reported.

Democratic political strategist J.J. Abbott called the Journal story “deeply disturbing.”

“My take: those of us who can’t do anything about John’s behavior — criticizing him ain’t gonna do it — should ignore him,” he wrote on X. “All else is going right for PA Dems to win power in Harrisburg and DC. Let’s focus on winning and not giving him what he wants.”

Fetterman’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Former Christian Reality Show Host Accused of Threatening to Kill Trump
entries.summary: Benjamin Azariah Southworth is accused of posting death threats on social media and harassing Trump’s personal lawyer.
entries.content:
Authorities arrested a former Christian reality show host this week in Los Angeles on federal charges of making threats to kill President Donald Trump, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California said in a news release.

Benjamin Azariah Southworth, 40, was charged with one count of threats against Trump, one count of cyberstalking and one count of harassing telephone calls in interstate communications, the release said. He was also accused of harassing Trump’s former personal lawyer and that lawyer’s family.

The president has faced a series of high-profile death threats and assasination attempts during the last few years, including an attack at a Pennsylvania rally in 2024 and a shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in April.

“As threats against President Trump’s life escalate, the Department of Justice will respond with the full force of the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement this week. “We will hold perpetrators of violent threats accountable, and anyone who makes these threats online will not be allowed to hide behind their screens.”

Southworth is accused of expressing hate toward Trump and his supporters through social media channels between January 2026 to May 2026, the U.S. attorney’s office said.

He is accused of sharing the address of Trump’s personal lawyer, as well as photos of their house. Southworth wrote “No peace for traitors” on the post, the release said. He is also accused of leaving “abusive messages” online and over voicemail to the lawyer’s son, as well as making a series of “harassing telephone calls” to the lawyer’s wife from January to May 2026.

He is accused of posting a video on April 7 to Instagram, where he said, “This government is illegitimate and out of control. It’s time for course correction. Kill Donald Trump.”

Southworth came out as gay in 2008 while hosting “The Remix,” a youth show that spotlighted Christian singers. He also co-hosted the “Yass, Jesus!” podcast from 2020 to 2024, which is described on streaming services as an “interfaith and sexuality affirming comedy podcast.”

He sells sticker sheets on his website of a sad hamster meme with the words “Kill Trump.”

If convicted, Southworth faces a maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the threats charge, five years for the cyberstalking charge and two years for the harassment charge.
